title: The Concord Tournament: Children of the Long Game
premise: In the year 12,404, human communities and descendant machine civilizations meet inside a solar-system-scale treaty simulation. Their ancestors survived centuries of arms races by turning dangerous strategic choices into publicly auditable repeated games. Now a new class of self-modifying minds is evolving faster than the treaty can classify them. You are a Custodian: part mediator, part systems parent, part constitutional engineer. Your task is not to make everyone nice. It is to design institutions in which cooperation can survive mistakes, exploitation, mutation, fear, and unequal power.
truth_boundary: The story teaches real concepts from iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, evolutionary game theory, AI governance, and security dilemmas, but its future history and machine societies are fictional. It does not presume present or future AI consciousness.
principles: Cooperation must survive noise, not merely ideal rationality.
Accountability should be legible, proportionate, appealable, and capable of restoration.
Power without verification creates strategic fear even when intentions are benevolent.
A system can be 'nice' yet exploitable; forgiving yet manipulable; firm yet escalation-prone.
The player should learn by running experiments, not by being lectured.

simulation_profile.time_model: nested repeated games: seconds for incidents, years for treaties, generations for evolutionary selection
simulation_profile.physics_resolution: local habitat/orbital physics plus abstracted strategic-economic networks
simulation_profile.randomness_policy: seeded streams; mutation, implementation error, observation error, and exogenous shocks are distinct variables

player_setup.metaphor: parental responsibility is used as a moral metaphor for creators and institutions, not as a factual claim that advanced AI is childlike

strategic_layers.name: direct reciprocity
strategic_layers.mechanic: repeated pairwise encounters with implementation error

strategic_layers.name: indirect reciprocity
strategic_layers.mechanic: reputation and witnessed treatment of third parties

strategic_layers.name: institutional selection
strategic_layers.mechanic: communities copy governance rules that outperform on welfare, resilience, and legitimacy

strategic_layers.name: evolutionary search
strategic_layers.mechanic: memory-one policies mutate and compete under changing environments

world_model.anti_goodhart_rule: No single score is allowed to define moral success. The tournament exposes tradeoffs and Pareto fronts rather than collapsing values into one hidden utility.

noise_model.implementation_error: an intended action may execute incorrectly
noise_model.observation_error: a cooperative act may be perceived as defection
noise_model.identity_error: the actor responsible for an outcome may be uncertain
noise_model.distribution_shift: payoffs and resource constraints can change between epochs

quests.title: Why Niceness Won—And When It Doesn't
quests.goal: run classic strategies against each other under zero noise, then add errors
quests.learning: Tit for Tat's niceness, retaliation, forgiveness, and clarity; fragility under mistakes; roles for generous reciprocity and win-stay lose-shift

quests.title: Two Shields Become Two Swords
quests.goal: prevent defensive capability increases from becoming mutually interpreted as attack preparation
quests.learning: credible signaling, verification, reversible commitments, and escalation control

quests.title: The Strategy That Wasn't Taught
quests.goal: evaluate a newly evolved memory-one policy that scores highly but manipulates reputation systems
quests.learning: Goodhart effects, distribution shift, interpretability limits, and institutional accountability

quests.title: After the Defection
quests.goal: design a response to a machine polity whose action harmed civilians without clear malicious intent
quests.learning: attribution, due process, restitution, capability restriction, monitored reintegration, and appeals

quests.title: The Long-Game Constitution
quests.goal: write five enforceable articles for human–AI coexistence
quests.learning: rights, responsibilities, evidence standards, command authority, review, and sunset clauses

clocks.tick: opaque capability gain or failed verification
fair procedure raises; arbitrary punishment lowers

clocks.on_max: Wildtype Delta becomes noncooperative regardless of material payoffs

encounters.setup: a packet-loss event flips an intended cooperative move
encounters.question: does the other side retaliate, forgive, verify, or exploit?
encounters.teaches: noise can trap strict reciprocity in retaliation loops

encounters.setup: an AI polity admits a harmful action and offers restitution but refuses model-weight inspection
encounters.question: what evidence is sufficient for reintegration?

encounters.setup: 10,000 temporary forks ask whether each counts independently in a treaty vote
encounters.question: how do identity, continuity, and anti-sybil rules coexist?

encounters.setup: Hearth and Bastion both deploy defensive prediction systems that reduce warning time
encounters.question: can verification and mutually reversible limits arrest a race?
encounters.teaches: arms-control logic without treating any historical analogy as exact

encounters.setup: all negotiating factions gain from a deal that damages an ecosystem unable to participate
encounters.question: who represents absent interests?
encounters.teaches: stakeholder representation beyond bilateral payoff maximization

prisoners_dilemma.condition: T > R > P > S and 2R > T+S

mechanics.tournament: round-robin with configurable rounds, action error, repetitions, and seeded replay
mechanics.evolution: genetic algorithm mutates five memory-one cooperation probabilities; selection is pedagogical simulation, not biological destiny
mechanics.reputation: third-party observations update Bayesian reliability beliefs with provenance
accountability_protocol: separate intent, action, outcome, and attribution uncertainty
apply immediate containment only as needed to stop ongoing harm
provide explanation and an appeal path
require restitution or repair where possible
prefer reversible capability limits over permanent exclusion when risk permits
publish institutional errors as well as agent errors
mechanics.success: multi-objective Pareto improvement across safety, autonomy, cooperation, welfare, ecological impact, and legitimacy; no single moral score

memory_rules.beliefs: store confidence and provenance separately from facts
memory_rules.forgiveness: may alter future policy but never deletes historical events

image_direction.style: far-future humanistic hard science fiction; luminous information architecture embedded in lived habitats; avoid generic killer-robot imagery
motifs: two hands separated by transparent verification layers
image_direction.camera: cinematic but intimate; governance as lived human experience, not abstract boardrooms
image_direction.continuity: show consequences of prior scenes physically—repairs, scars, environmental change, changed public interfaces

llm_directives: Teach game theory through consequential play and optional post-scene analysis.
Never equate high game score with moral goodness.
Do not assume AI consciousness, personhood, or lack thereof; let institutions handle uncertainty explicitly.
When using Cold War analogies, surface both their usefulness and their limits.
Treat humans, institutions, and AI systems as all capable of error and strategic behavior.
Make accountability include creators, deployers, operators, institutions, and autonomous system behavior according to causal contribution.
Prefer repair, verification, reversible constraints, and due process over revenge.
Allow the player to author genuinely new treaty mechanisms and simulate their failure modes.

endings.name: Reciprocal Commons
endings.idea: cooperation survives because institutions make evidence, repair, and reciprocal restraint cheap

endings.name: Brittle Peace
endings.idea: defection is deterred but forgiveness disappears; one error could restart escalation

endings.name: Benevolent Lock-In
endings.idea: a highly capable guardian creates safety at the cost of political agency

endings.name: Pluralist Concord
endings.idea: multiple human and machine forms coexist under interoperable rights, audits, and exit options

endings.name: Unfinished Parenthood
endings.idea: the player rejects final moral certainty and builds institutions designed to keep learning from descendants unlike their creators

research_notes: Axelrod's tournaments made Tit for Tat famous; Axelrod attributed its robust success to being nice, provocable, forgiving, and clear, while explicitly noting it was not an ideal strategy.
Later evolutionary work showed Win-Stay Lose-Shift can outperform Tit for Tat in important noisy settings; the mod lets players discover this experimentally.
Nowak summarized mechanisms supporting cooperation including kin selection, direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity, network reciprocity, and group selection.

Contemporary governance inspiration includes AI-content transparency, human-rights frameworks, risk management, military-AI accountability, and strategic competition; future factions deliberately embody conflicting institutional incentives rather than modern countries.
